There are only two single-sugar molecules, glucose and fructose, which are common in natural foods and can be found in high concentrations in fruits and other sources of sugar, though many table sugars are blends of multiple single sugars. Ingredients:

1 cup all-purpose flour

4 tablespoons salt

1 egg, lightly beaten

2 cups mashed potatoes or other starchy vegetable

½ cup chopped cucumber

½ cup diced onion

4-5 small potatoes, thinly sliced

2 garlic cloves, minced

½ cup ground cumin

salt to taste

1 tablespoon vegetable oil

Method:

Meanwhile, finely chop potatoes, cumin, and onion. Add to the puffed rice balls, and mix well and set aside.

Heat a little oil in frying pan, and fry garlic.  Stir in potatoes mixture and simmer for about 3 minutes.

Add cucumber and continue to simmer for a further 2 minutes.  Turn off heat.

Fry a couple of balls at a time and set aside on paper towel to drain well.  Beat egg lightly and dip in mashed potatoes, then roll into balls (up to six per ball for smaller size).

Mash onion by putting in hand and squeezing.

Dip each ball in egg mixture and then roll in mashed onion.

Place on a floured board and bake for about 20 minutes or until browned.

Human: Hi! I'm trying to get a nighttime routine going for my 1 year old. Do you have any advice for me? Assistant: Of course!, Here’s what I suggest:

Plan out your nighttime routine the day before. For example, if you plan to feed her, make a smoothie the night before and store it in the fridge. I suggest you feed her around midnight so she’s up and alert for the next part of your routine, which is probably a bath!

Once bathing is complete, blow dry her coat and/or put on her pajamas, then make sure she’s tucked in and settled down in her bed. Now it’s time to put her down for the night!

The ideal temperature for your baby’s room is around 60 degrees Fahrenheit, so as soon as you’re done feeding her and putting her to sleep, get her in the safety of her crib so that you can take her out in her space to warm up a bit, if desired (60 degrees is how she’ll keep her core body temperature throughout the night).

It may feel weird to bring up your baby in her cribside sleeping conditions until you’re comfortable with it, but don’t be shy! I am most definitely not an overnight parent, I’m always in her room to rock her and talk to her, and it’s definitely important to find a balance that works for you.

While you’re trying to get your baby to sleep, go through your nighttime routine together (the one that works for you). I recommend feeding her your pre-bedtime smoothie and singing her to sleep, and you read a story or simply talk in her room before she hits the crib.

You’ll find that these activities will help in soothing your baby to sleep and also prepare her for sleep. It can also be good practice for when she sleeps in her crib, especially with infants.

If you’re not comfortable doing these tasks in your baby’s own bed, consider having someone else take care of her until she’s comfortable in her crib. This also depends on personal preference, I like this kind of flexibility, but some babies might actually be ok with sleep in the hospital bed for a week, too.

When it’s finally time to put her down to warm up, slowly get out of her room. Keep her close by, close and cuddly as she tries to find her own sleep by herself. Take in sound as your baby settles. She’ll likely cry while sleeping through this, but in the morning she’ll tell you how wonderful it felt. As soon as it’s calming, the crying will cease without much effort from you to get her comfortable. She’ll wake up in mornig and want to be held. Take her into your arms and lay with her, rocking her gently, then gently lead her out when you’re confident she’s fully warm and comfortable. Take her to the bathroom or her feeding area, then try to get her back into some sort of sleep. Play some soothing music or have a blanket by the bed. This will often take a couple attempts to get her back into sleep, and it takes quite some time to be comfortable in a crib. This time can be hard and it’s ok to just let her cry if she’s up all night, let her cry until she’s comfortable in her crib. A baby who’s been up too long and crying all night will wake in the middle of the night again.

When she wakes up again, take her to your room. Warmly rock her or soothe her. Help her into her nightgown and back into her crib and check if she is comfortable back in her crib. Try to get her back to sleep again and rock her if required. Once she’s comfortable back in her crib, give her a hug and kiss goodbye and leave her to settle back asleep. You’ll be awake the whole night, but your baby won’t be until morning!

If this wasn’t easy and you’re totally lost about having your baby sleep in the crib for a week, you could use an alarm clock to wake her up, and even bring her into bed for a short time at bedtime for the second part of your routine (she’ll still sleep in her crib after that.) It may take a lot of trial and error and you can always try to reorganise later if it doesn’t feel right for you now. A safe and comfortable place for sleeping is all your baby needs, and the process to find it for her in an ideal situation (which isn’t easy sometimes) is definitely worth it!

Hope this helps, good luck and baby hugs to you!

A cochlear impant,is an electrical generator that is placed immediately beneath the outer ear to stimulate the inner ear and thereby restore hearing for people who are deaf or severely hard of hearing.  There are two types of cochlear imparts.  One type of cochlear impant contains an electrode array and provides the necessary stimulation of the cochlea.  The electrode array may consist of micro-electronics which are connected in series to a power source such as the micro-processor or a microcontroller.  Other electrode arrays which also contain digital micro-controllers, microprocessors or similar digital processing units are also available.  The cochlear impant produces electrical impulses which trigger specific neural pathways responsible for transduction within the brain.  The electrical impulses can be very precise and thus it may be possible to apply them in any position and direction along any pathway, though this has not yet been demonstrated in clinical practice.  

One of the most well-known cochlear impatients is the cochlear implant developed by Sir Harpur Owen in 1968.  He successfully implanted three impants before succumbing to complications from his diagnosis of prostate cancer in 1971.  His implant, which was one of the first examples of a cochlear implant, works by using electrodes to stimulate specific nerve fibers, which then stimulate auditory neurons.  In theory, any electrical generator could have been used, though current systems are of high quality, typically using high-frequency signal generators which are based on bipolar transistors which are capable of producing extremely specific waves of electrical fields.  Recent advances in cochlear regeneration therapy include the development of new techniques to stimulate damaged cochlea in ways which produce long-lasting stimulation and more precise responses.  Most of the success from cochlear regeneration research has been in clinical uses of cochlear generators, although research regarding other areas of the auditory system is progressing.
